extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of literature; readers studying early 20th-century American poets, dramatists, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and directed questions for reading and evaluating the works of early 20th-century authors (poets, dramatists, essayists) — prompts to analyze influences, technique, originality, rhythm, themes, and historical/contextual effects. Intended to structure classroom or self-directed study of individual writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read poems aloud to assess effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The poems need to be read aloud to give the full effect of their passion and lyric beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for passion, vocal rhythm, and lyric beauty that may be lost on silent reading; use oral performance to judge tonal and musical qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate naïveté: philosophy vs emotion (Millay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare Miss Millay's naïveté with that of Blake. Do you find suggestions of philosophy behind it or sheer emotion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast Millay's naïveté with Blake's to determine whether underlying philosophical ideas or raw feeling drive the poetry; cite poem examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess later-work development (Millay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does Miss Millay's later work show growth toward greatness or toward sophisticated cleverness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge later poems for signs of maturation (depth, originality) versus mere technical cleverness or artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess life-experience influence (O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: What effect has Mr. O'Neill's life experience had upon the quality of his plays?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate biographical episodes (sea voyages, work, illness, Provincetown life) to themes, character realism, and dramatic situations in his plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate originality across themes/background/technique (O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: What evidence of originality do you find in his (1) themes, (2) background, and (3) technique?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine specific plays for unique thematic choices, unusual settings or personal backgrounds used, and distinctive technical devices; give concrete examples for each of the three aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify specific literary influences (O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the influence of Joseph Conrad (cf. Manly and Rickert, Contemporary British Literature) upon O'Neill. Read especially The Nigger of the "Narcissus."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Conrad's thematic/atmospheric techniques and narrative concerns with those in O'Neill's plays to trace lines of influence; read the recommended Conrad text for direct comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess influence of Synge (O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: How has Mr. O'Neill been influenced by the plays of John Millington Synge?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare O'Neill's use of vernacular, rural settings, and dramatic structure with Synge's plays; identify shared motifs or divergences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate range vs specialization (O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: What do you make of the fact that Mr. O'Neill has struck out in various directions instead of working a particular vein?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider advantages and disadvantages of thematic and stylistic breadth versus concentrated mastery; assess consistency and cohesion across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh promise and limitations (O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: What reasons do you find for the common opinion that he is our most promising dramatist? What limitations or weaknesses do you think may interfere with his development? Do you think he will become a great dramatist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List evidence supporting his promise (awards, critical reception, innovations) and contrast with perceived weaknesses; predict likely trajectory with justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Pound chronologically to trace changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Pound is an experimenter in verse, who has come under many influences and belonged to many schools. His work should be studied chronologically to discover these changes in interest and relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read Pound's output in chronological order to observe shifts in style, technique, and affiliations; map phases and turning points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Pound's range of influences
rubrics_metrics.description: To be noted among the influences are: (1) the mediæval poetry of Provence; (2) the Greek poets; (3) the Latin poets of the Empire; (4) among modern French poets, Laurent Tailhade; (5) the poets of China and Japan, whom he learned to know through the manuscript notes of Ernest Fenollosa; (6) the work of the English Imagists (cf. especially the poems of T.E. Hulme, published in Mr. Pound's volume called Ripostes); (7) the work of the Vorticist school of poets and artists (cf. Blast, edited by Wyndham Lewis), and the more accessible periodical, The Egoist, of which Richard Aldington is assistant editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying Pound, explicitly look for traces of these listed influences in form, diction, imagery, and theoretical statements; annotate examples linking specific influences to passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate Pound's stated theory to his poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider also this from his own theory of poetry: "Poetry is a sort of inspired mathematics, which gives us equations, not for abstract figures, triangles, spheres and the like, but equations for the human emotions. If one have a mind which inclines to magic rather than science, one will prefer to speak of these equations as spells or incantations; it sounds more arcane, mysterious, recondite." Can this be related to the qualities of Mr. Pound's poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare theoretical statements to concrete poems: look for precise, 'mathematical' structuring of emotion and for any magical/arcane stylistic devices that realize the metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate content vs form critique in Pound's work
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading Mr. Pound's output, discuss the adequacy of the following: "When content has become for an artist merely something to inflate and display form with, then the petty serves as well as the great, the ignoble equally with the lofty, the unlovely like the beautiful, the sordid as the clean.... Real feeling consequently becomes rarer, and the artist descends to trivialities of observation, vagaries of assertion, or mere bravado of standards and expression--pure tilting at convention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether Pound's work exemplifies or rebuts this criticism about form displacing content; cite poems illustrating either tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess primary influences before judging Oppenheim
rubrics_metrics.description: The following influences have entered largely into Oppenheim's work: Whitman, the Bible, and the theories of psycho-analysis developed by Freud and Jung. Without considering these, no fair estimate of the value of his work can be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify elements traceable to Whitman, biblical language/themes, and psychoanalytic theory; incorporate these when evaluating Oppenheim's value and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Oriental temperament in Oppenheim's poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In what respects does his poetry reflect the Oriental temperament?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for formal, thematic, or tonal traits often associated with 'Oriental' poetics (imagery, restraint, tonal qualities) and give textual examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify strengths and weaknesses (Oppenheim)
rubrics_metrics.description: What strength do you find in his work? what weakness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a balanced critique listing notable strengths (voice, imagery, theme) and weaknesses (mannerism, inconsistency), with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use critical reviews as entry points (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good introduction to Mr. Robinson's work is Miss Lowell's review of his Collected Works ... Although Miss Lowell's contention that Mr. Robinson is our greatest living poet would be disputed by some critics, her article suggests many points of departure in the study of his very important contribution to American poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult recommended critical reviews to frame initial questions and departure points for your own reading and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify material source and assess endurance (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide Mr. Robinson's work into two groups: (1) poems of which the material is based upon literature; (2) those of which it comes from his own life experience. Is it possible to say now which of these two groups has the best chance of long endurance? Can you decide how far literature has had a good effect upon Mr. Robinson's work, and how far it has lessened the value of his poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sort poems by source, compare lasting qualities of each group, and judge whether literary borrowing enhances or detracts from poetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess regional (New England) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider as a group the poems that grow out of Mr. Robinson's New England origin. In what ways is he characteristic of New England? Compare his work with that of Mr. Frost in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify regional themes, language, moral tone, and landscape representation; perform a comparative analysis with Frost's regionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare portrait-poems with Spoon River
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare and contrast Mr. Robinson's portraits of persons with names as titles with similar portraits in the Spoon River Anthology. This type of verse seems to have been developed independently by both poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze structure, voice, ironic distance, and characterization in Robinson's titled-person poems versus Spoon River pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace influence of Crabbe and Hardy (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interesting study could be made of the influence on Robinson of Crabbe; another, of the influence of Hardy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate thematic, tonal, or formal parallels between Robinson and Crabbe/Hardy; cite specific poems that show these influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess impact of delayed recognition (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another interesting study might grow out of the consideration of Robinson as a poet born twenty years too soon. How much has the temper of his work been determined by the fact that he had to wait so long for recognition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider psychological and tonal effects of late recognition: bitterness, restraint, maturity; correlate with biographical timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract philosophical features from poems (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the main features of Mr. Robinson's philosophy as suggested in the poems?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring worldview elements (pessimism/optimism, moralism, humanism) and support with textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate musicality and mastery of rhythm (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you find many poems that sing? What is to be said of the poet's mastery of rhythms?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metrical control, melodic line, and rhythmic variation; cite poems demonstrating strong musical qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare your judgment with critical praise (Robinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the best of Mr. Robinson's work, it is interesting to look up the comments of various admirers ... and to see how far your judgment bears out these extravagant statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast your reading with contemporary critical tributes; note agreements and points of divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Robinson's influence on later poets
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of Robinson's work on younger American poets, especially on Lindsay and Sandburg, makes an interesting study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace stylistic, thematic, or formal echoes in the work of Lindsay and Sandburg attributable to Robinson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess theory of freedom from conventions (Sandburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging Mr. Sandburg's work, it is important to remember that his theory involves complete freedom from conventions of all sorts--in thinking, in metrical form, and in vocabulary. His aim seems to be to reproduce the impressions that all phases of life make upon him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Sandburg's poems in light of intentional anti-conventionalism; determine whether freedom produces authenticity or formlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess environmental influence on imagination (Sandburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether his early prairie environment had anything to do with the large scale of his imagination, the appeal to him of enormous periods of time, masses of men, and forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link biographical/environmental context (prairie life) to thematic scale, scope, and imagery in his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine universality within localism (Sandburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find elements of universality in his exaggerated localisms? Do they combine to form a definite philosophy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether local, concrete detail transcends parochialism to express universal concerns; consider whether this coheres into an articulated philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge formal eccentricities as expression or blemish (Sandburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: What effect do the eccentricities and crudities of form have upon you? Do you consider them an essential part of his poetic expression or blemishes which he may one day overcome?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether unconventional forms serve expressive aims or are technical defects; substantiate with poem examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh elements of greatness against defects (Sandburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find elements of greatness in Mr. Sandburg's work? Do you think they are likely to outweigh his obvious defects?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance significant strengths (vision, scope, voice) against defects (crudity, unevenness) and judge overall lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare democratic ideals with other poets (Sandburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare and contrast his democratic ideals with those of Lindsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze thematic representations of democracy, populism, and social values in Sandburg and Lindsay; note convergences and divergences.
